name: EMA and the European AI Network
blurb: How European regulators are organising their own AI use.
title: EMA and the European AI Network
answer: The EMA and the national agencies coordinate AI through a network data steering group and publish an annual AI observatory report. The 2025 report described the year as the point where regulators' use of AI moved from adoption to practical application, while noting it records activity rather than setting requirements.

reading.body:
The EMA coordinates AI across European medicines regulators through a network data steering group, and its 2025 observatory report described the year as the shift from adoption to practical application.

That framing matters because it separates two things regulators often blur. The reflection paper, adopted in September 2024, is the network's statement to industry: a risk based approach, early engagement through scientific advice or qualification, and documentation of data, models and validation across discovery, clinical development, authorisation, manufacturing and post-authorisation safety. The observatory report is the network's account of its own AI use. One sets expectations for developers, the other records what regulators are doing and watching.

The reflection paper is explicitly not binding. It sets out current thinking, and the observatory report records activity rather than requirements. A team that treats either as a compliance checklist will misread both. The practical instruction the data supports is narrower: when AI is central to the evidence, engage the EMA early through scientific advice.

What this does not cover is the compute, buildings or power behind any of it. The data describes governance and coordination, not infrastructure, and nothing here indicates how much compute the network or the developers it regulates consume. It also does not say what the 2025 report found beyond the adoption to application shift, or which technologies it flagged. The related Digital Omnibus entry sits alongside this material, but the data given does not connect the two.

The network's two outputs serve different audiences and carry different force. The reflection paper is addressed outward to developers and is explicitly non-binding. The observatory report is addressed inward, an account of what regulators themselves are doing. A developer reading the observatory report for compliance signals is reading the wrong document, and a regulator reading the reflection paper as a rulebook is doing the same.

The coordination structure is the part that travels. A data steering group plus a multiannual AI workplan plus an annual observatory report is a mechanism for keeping twenty-plus national authorities pointed in the same direction without issuing binding law. That is why the reflection paper can cover the whole lifecycle from discovery to post-authorisation safety while setting no requirements. The network is aligning expectations first and legislating later, if at all.

The one actionable instruction in the data is timing. When AI is central to the evidence, the reflection paper recommends engaging the EMA early through scientific advice, or through a qualification procedure when the method is meant for wider use. Both routes exist before submission, which means the cost of asking is paid early and the cost of not asking is paid at review.

How do I get EMA feedback on an AI method?
Through scientific advice for a specific product, or through a qualification procedure for a method intended for wider use.

Does the reflection paper set requirements?
No. It sets out the agency's current thinking and expectations, not binding legal requirements.

What did the 2025 AI Observatory report actually find?
The data records only that it described the year as the point where regulators' use of AI moved from adoption to practical application. It does not say which technologies the report flagged or what else it concluded.

When was the reflection paper adopted?
September 2024.

Does the network's AI work cover manufacturing and post-authorisation safety?
Yes. The reflection paper covers AI from discovery through clinical development, authorisation, manufacturing and post-authorisation safety.

Is the observatory report a compliance document?
No. It records activity rather than setting requirements, and it tracks how regulators themselves are using AI and which technologies they are watching.

How does the Digital Omnibus relate to this network?
The data does not connect them. The Digital Omnibus entry sits alongside this material as a related term, but nothing given here establishes a relationship.

explainer:
The European medicines regulatory network is the EMA together with the national competent authorities of EU and EEA countries. It coordinates AI through a data steering group and a multiannual AI workplan, covering guidance for industry, regulators' own use of AI, collaboration with international partners, and experimentation.

The EMA's reflection paper is the network's main statement to industry. It covers AI from discovery through clinical development, authorisation, manufacturing and post-authorisation safety, and asks developers to take a risk based approach, to discuss novel uses with regulators early through scientific advice or qualification procedures, and to document data, models and validation. The network's annual AI observatory report tracks how regulators themselves are using AI and which technologies they are watching, and it is a useful signal of where future guidance may go.

What the European network is

Medicines regulation in Europe is shared between the European Medicines Agency and the national agencies of the member states, which together form a network. Decisions on new medicines are made by committees drawn from across it, assessments are done by national teams, and inspections are run nationally. When the network adopts a position on AI, it sets expectations for every company submitting in Europe and for every agency in the system.

What the network has done on AI

The agencies have published a joint workplan on AI, a reflection paper on the use of AI across the medicine lifecycle, and guiding principles for their own use of large language models. The reflection paper takes a risk based view: AI used in early discovery needs little regulatory attention, while AI that influences a decision about a medicine's benefits, risks or quality needs evidence proportionate to that influence, and sponsors are encouraged to discuss their plans with the agencies early. The workplan also covers how the agencies will build their own capability and share experience across the network.

What it means for companies

A company planning to use AI in a European submission can expect assessors to ask what the model did, how it was validated for that use, and how its limitations were handled, and it can expect those questions to be asked consistently across member states. The scientific advice route lets sponsors raise novel uses before committing to them. Because the EU AI Act applies alongside medicines law, companies also need to know which of its obligations a given use triggers, a question the network has said it will help clarify.
